source: Ireland & Bundy (1992) Using failure to guide inductive proof (Edinburgh DAI RP 613)
finding: A proof plan has a method (declarative preconditions and effects) and a tactic (the guaranteed inference steps). Methods can fail. Each method gets critics: a critic has preconditions that name an interesting failure, and effects that say how to patch it. This is the founding idea of repair by plan.
numbers: Worked example: rev(rev(v)<>w::nil)=w::v. Plain induction gets stuck on partial terms in the induction conclusion. The fix needs one lemma (A<>(B::C)=(A<>B::nil)<>C) and one generalisation (forall v,w: rev(rev(v)<>w)=rev(w)<>v).
quote: Rippling provides a high-level explanation of how to control the search for a proof.
limits: Prototype only. The paper says the critics implementation is under way in lambda-Prolog. No success rate on a benchmark. Only 5 example theorems.
agent_relevance: Repair is driven by a named failure type that the plan can see, not by free guessing. Our S5 REVISE could key patches to the type of failed check.

source: Ireland & Bundy (1992) Using failure to guide inductive proof (Edinburgh DAI RP 613)
finding: Failure of rippling (the step-case rewrite gets blocked) is used to focus the search for lemmas and generalisations. Four critic kinds: lemma calculation, lemma speculation, generalisation, and sink generalisation. The speculation critic can call the calculation critic inside it.
numbers: Table 1 lists 5 example theorems (even(x+x); (x+y)-x=(y+x)-x; rev(rev(x<>y)); rotate(length(x),x<>y); rev(rev(x)<>y::nil)=y::x). Table 2 lists which of calculation, speculation, generalisation each needed. Strategy for higher-order unification: pick the most general unifier that preserves skeleton term structure.
limits: No timing, no failure count. Control of higher-order unification was the main engineering result. Baseline is the Boyer-Moore prover heuristics (cross-fertilisation, generalisation), which it claims to extend.
agent_relevance: A failed attempt carries structure (which step blocked, what was left over). Keep that residue as the input to repair, not just the error text.

source: Ireland & Bundy (1996) Productive use of failure in inductive proof, J. Automated Reasoning 16(1-2)
finding: Journal version of the critics work. Proposes an architecture that finds eureka steps (missing lemmas, generalisations) automatically from the failure of rippling.
numbers: Not read in full. Only the abstract and bibliographic record were seen via search.
limits: PDF not reachable (Edinburgh repository returns 403). Claims on results here are unverified.
agent_relevance: Cite as the standard reference for critics. Read the full text before using any number from it.

source: Bundy (1988) The use of explicit plans to guide inductive proofs, CADE-9
finding: Original proof planning proposal: describe a proof strategy as a plan made of methods, so the prover can reason about the proof at a high level. Cited by Ireland & Bundy 1992 as the source of the idea; the CLAM planner implements it.
numbers: No numbers read this session. Seen only as a citation in rp613 and in the Ringer et al. survey.
limits: Primary text not opened (could not retrieve). Treat details as second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary (plan, method, tactic, critic) for a code-run REVISE state: the plan names what the failed step was supposed to do.

source: Ringer, Palmskog, Sergey, Gligoric, Tatlock (2020) QED at Large: a survey of engineering of formally verified software
finding: The survey places proof planning critics (Ireland 1996) as a form of proof repair. It defines proof repair as program repair for proofs and notes the key advantage: a specification (the theorem statement) is always available to check the patch.
numbers: Section 7.2.3. Names PUMPKIN PATCH (Ringer 2018), Chick (Robert 2018), RefactorAgda, proof weaving (Mulhern 2006), GALILEO (Chan 2011) as repair techniques. Says a program repair review (Qi et al. 2015) found many tools give incorrect patches.
quote: In proof repair, a specification is always available: the theorem the repaired proof ought to prove.
limits: A survey, not an experiment. Says only preliminary tooling exists and PUMPKIN PATCH handles only simple changes.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails G2 and G3: a repair is trusted only when an independent checker accepts it. The theorem statement is the check.

source: Ringer et al. (2020) QED at Large - proof planning paragraph
finding: Proof planning (Bundy 1988) uses plans to guide search for proofs with similar structure. Critics reuse information from failing proofs. It started in automated provers and reached interactive provers via IsaPlanner (Dixon & Fleuriot 2003, rippling in Isabelle) and a rippling tool for Coq.
numbers: Proof reuse section of the survey (6.4).
limits: Brief survey text. No measured results.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea moved from fully automatic provers into human-in-loop tools: the plan layer is reusable around any checker.

source: Ringer, Porter, Yazdani, Leo, Grossman (2021) Proof Repair across Type Equivalences (PLDI)
finding: Pumpkin Pi repairs broken Coq proofs when a type changes. It runs a configurable proof-term transformation (transport along an equivalence) and then a decompiler turns the new proof term into a suggested tactic script. The old type is removed from the repaired term and no extra axioms are needed.
numbers: Eight case studies (Table 1): algebraic ornaments (list to packed vector), unpack sigma types, tuples and records, permute constructors, add constructors, factor constructors, permute hypotheses, change inductive structure (unary to binary). The industrial proof engineer rarely waited more than ten seconds, so aggressive caching was added.
limits: Case studies, not a controlled experiment. Authors say savings were on the order of minutes for small developments and none when adding constructors. Suggested tactics sometimes needed massaging. The decompiler deliberately gives up soundness for readable tactics.
agent_relevance: Repair works best when the change is a known kind and the fix is a mechanical transformation, with the checker closing the loop. Suggests classifying the change before repairing (S5).

source: Ringer et al. (2021) Proof Repair across Type Equivalences - user-study link
finding: Benchmarks came from the REPLica user study of proof engineers. Swapping two constructors of a language was repaired fully by Pumpkin Pi with a human choosing the permutation from a list of suggestions. Adding a constructor gave no time saving over the study engineer.
numbers: One benchmark change: swap two constructors in Term and add a Bool constructor. Automatic configuration for the swap; manual plus automatic for the addition. Factoring constructors: savings of minutes on a small development.
limits: The REPLica user study itself was not opened, only cited. No N or timings from it were read.
agent_relevance: A human-in-loop pick of the repair plan from a short ranked list is cheap. Our agent could let code enumerate repair plans and let the model only choose.

source: First, Rabe, Ringer, Brun (2023) Baldur: whole-proof generation and repair with LLMs (FSE)
finding: Baldur fine-tunes a Minerva LLM (8B and 62B) to write a whole Isabelle/HOL proof in one shot. A second model takes theorem + failed proof + Isabelle error message and writes a repaired proof.
numbers: PISA test set, 6,336 theorems. Whole-proof 8B: 34.8% with 16 samples, 40.7% with 64. With context, 8B: 36.3% (16) and 47.5% (64); 62B with context: 40.9% and 47.9%. Sledgehammer 25.6%; search-based LM 39.0%. Baldur combined with Thor 65.7%. One repair attempt on each failed greedy proof added 266 theorems (4.2%).
limits: Minerva pretraining may contain Isabelle proofs from the test set (leak risk, authors say so). The repair gain is compared at equal inference cost in the next line.
agent_relevance: Whole-proof then repair from the checker's error is a workable loop and beats search at similar cost.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur - repair ablation (error message)
finding: Key control: a repair model trained without the error message did not beat plain re-sampling at equal inference cost. The model with the error message did. So the gain comes from the error text, not from a second try.
numbers: Figure 5: ratio proved vs. number of attempts (0 to 30). Generate+Repair above Generate; Generate+Repair (no error message) does not surpass Generate when cost is normalised. Repair uses deduplicated failed proofs, one repair per failure, temperature 0.
quote: the information in the error message is crucial for the observed gains of the repair approach
limits: Read from a figure legend and the text; exact curve values were not extracted. Single benchmark, Isabelle only.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 directly: repair must cite real checker output. Without that, repair is just more sampling.

source: Lu, Delaware, Zhang (2024) Proof Automation with LLMs (PALM), ASE
finding: Formative study of GPT-3.5 Coq proof errors: the model usually gets the high-level proof structure right and the low-level details wrong. PALM generates a proof, then repairs it with targeted symbolic repair rules and CoqHammer, with backtracking.
numbers: Error study (520 errors by the abstract, 579 theorems analysed): wrong theorem application 49.6%, invalid reference 15.2%, incorrect rewrite 11.7%, redundant intros 10.8%, tactic misuse 8.5%, bullet misuse 3.7%, other 0.6%. Dataset: more than 10K theorems from 27 Coq projects.
limits: The counts 520 (abstract) and 579 (intro) differ; both come from the authors. The GPT-3.5 error mix may not hold for newer models.
agent_relevance: Errors fall into a few types, so a small typed set of repair rules covers most. The plan stays right while details break: repair details, keep the plan.

source: Lu et al. (2024) PALM results and ablation
finding: PALM (GPT-3.5) proved 4,377 theorems (40.4%). It beat Passport 14.4%, Proverbot9001 17.1% and DSP 22.9% (no repair). Gains of 180.4%, 136.7%, 76.6%. It proved 1,270 theorems no baseline proved.
numbers: GPT-3.5 alone 402 (3.7%); GPT-4o alone 689 (6.4%) vs PALM+GPT-4o 4,614 (42.6%); Llama-3-70B alone 386 (3.6%) vs PALM 4,155 (38.3%); Llama-3-8B 7 (0.1%) vs 3,433 (31.7%). Dropping one repair rule costs 3.0-6.9 points. Variant without CoqHammer: 702 (6.5%). Successful CoqHammer calls average 4.3 s.
limits: Most of the lift is CoqHammer, not the repair rules: removing it drops PALM to 6.5%. DSP is compared with its own prompting setup. PALM still fails on 59.6% of theorems.
agent_relevance: The big win is the symbolic fixer, not the LLM. A weak generator plus a strong code-run fixer beats a stronger generator alone (GPT-4o 6.4% vs PALM with GPT-3.5 40.4%).

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (ICLR)
finding: Plan then fill: an LLM drafts an informal proof, maps it to a formal sketch with open gaps, and an off-the-shelf prover (Sledgehammer plus heuristics) closes the gaps. This is a proof plan made by an LLM and checked by a prover.
numbers: miniF2F-test (Isabelle): Sledgehammer + heuristics 20.9% (abstract: 20.9% to 39.3% with DSP); Thor + expert iteration 39.3%; DSP with human informal proofs 39.3% on test; DSP with Minerva informal proofs on test: 8B 36.5%, 62B 34.0%, 540B 30.3%. 20 hand-written sketch examples as prompt.
limits: Test accuracy falls as the informal-proof model grows (36.5 to 30.3); the paper does not explain this well. The results table was garbled in text extraction, so row labels were reconstructed.
agent_relevance: A plan made of sub-claims whose gaps are filled by a checker is the template for our plan-then-revise flow.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) DSP ablations
finding: Each part helps. Removing the in-line comments that link informal to formal costs 4.9 (valid) and 2.8 (test) points. Removing informal proofs costs 3.7 and 5.3. Replacing sketches by full formal proofs (no prover to close gaps) costs 9.8 and 9.0.
numbers: Drops versus DSP with human informal proofs (valid/test, as stated in the text): in-line comments -4.9/-2.8; informal proofs -3.7/-5.3; automated provers -9.8/-9.0. The table lists 37.7% for one test ablation and 32.8% for the no-prover one.
limits: Single benchmark, one prover back-end. Text drops and table values were not fully reconciled.
agent_relevance: The biggest loss comes from removing the checker-filled gaps. A plan without a closing checker loses most of its value.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: neural theorem proving with growing libraries
finding: The prover writes modular proofs using skills (verified lemmas) from a growing library; an evolver rewrites skills to be reusable. The library grows during proving.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 48.0% to 57.0%; miniF2F-test 45.5% to 50.0%. Over 20,000 new skills generated. Ablation: new skills lift success from 47.1% to 50.4%.
limits: Gains are on Isabelle miniF2F only. Leak risk was not examined in the lines read.
agent_relevance: Repair by decomposing into verified lemmas that persist. Helps S5 only if lemmas are kept between attempts.

source: Lyra authors (2023) Lyra: orchestrating dual correction in automated theorem proving
finding: Two repair steps on top of DSP. Tool Correction replaces a failing proof tool (e.g. simp) with other tools such as Sledgehammer when the claim is right but the tool is weak. Conjecture Correction feeds the previous sketch and the prover's error back to the LLM to rewrite the sketch.
numbers: miniF2F (Isabelle), GPT-4 sketches. With human informal proofs: valid 55.3%, test 51.2% (previous best 48.0 and 45.5; DSP +12.7 and +11.9). With GPT-4 informal proofs: 54.9% and 47.9%. At 100 attempts vs 540B-Minerva DSP: valid 42.6 to 52.8, test 38.9 to 44.2. Tool Correction adds 4.1 (GPT-4 proofs) or 3.3 (human) points on test without Conjecture Correction; 7.0 and 8.2 with it.
limits: Conjecture Correction needs more attempts (200 vs 100). Table 2 was garbled in extraction so each row's flags were reconstructed from the text.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of repair, fix the tool versus fix the claim, have separate gains. A model for two REVISE operators.

source: Thakur et al. (2024) COPRA: in-context learning agent for formal theorem proving (COLM)
finding: GPT-4 proposes one tactic at a time, the prover runs it, and on an error the error message and proof state go back into the prompt. A stateful backtracking search drops failed branches and keeps a history.
numbers: miniF2F-test (Lean), 60 queries: few-shot GPT-4 13.52%; COPRA 26.63%; COPRA minus backtracking 24.59%; plus retrieval 29.09%; plus retrieval and informal proof 29.92%; 100 queries 30.74%. REPROVER (fine-tuned) 25.00%; Llemma-7b 26.23%. Few-shot at T=0.7 with 60 attempts 15.98%. COPRA finds proofs about 3x faster than ReProver with 16x fewer queries.
limits: The table was garbled in extraction; the row-to-number mapping is reconstructed, so check the PDF before quoting. Needs GPT-4 (COPRA with GPT-3.5 9.02%, CodeLlama 5.73%). Compared with ReProver at different query counts.
agent_relevance: Backtracking is worth about 2 points over linear repair; error feedback plus state in the prompt roughly doubles the few-shot baseline.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2024/2026) Cobblestone: divide-and-conquer proof synthesis
finding: An LLM writes full proofs; code runs them, finds which prefix and subproofs succeed, replaces the first failing tactic with admit, and recurses only on the unproven subgoals. Pieces are combined into a sound proof.
numbers: CoqGym100: Cobblestone 48%, CoqHammer 30%, Proverbot9001 17%, chain-of-thought baseline 25%. coq-wigderson100: 38% vs 27%, 10%, 19%. Tokens per theorem: 59.3K vs 99.3K for LinearRegen (CoqGym100). Run cost about $1.46 and 15.3 min. Proves 46 theorems all non-LLM tools miss; 14 the other way; 127 both. Up to 58% with an oracle giving structure.
limits: Leak control used newer projects (PnVRocqLib, coq-bb5). Rango and Tactician could not run on some datasets (N/A). COPRA was not compared (cost).
agent_relevance: Keep the good prefix and repair only the failing subgoal. Maps onto S5: localise the failure with code before asking the model.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango: adaptive retrieval-augmented proving for software verification
finding: Fine-tuned Coq prover that retrieves similar proofs and premises at every step. Introduces CoqStoq (2,226 Coq projects, 196,929 theorems).
numbers: Abstract read: 32.0% of benchmark theorems, 29% more than the previous state of the art.
limits: Only the first page was read. No repair loop. Included as the retrieval baseline in the Cobblestone and PALM comparisons.
agent_relevance: Baseline context only. Retrieval is a different lever than repair.

source: Ren et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2: RL for subgoal decomposition
finding: A large model (DeepSeek-V3) decomposes a theorem into subgoals written as Lean have-statements with sorry; a 7B prover solves each subgoal; solved parts are stitched into a chain-of-thought that cold-starts RL. Plan first, fill after.
numbers: MiniF2F-test: 82.4% at pass@32 and 88.9% at pass@8192 (671B). PutnamBench 47 of 658 (pass@1024). ProverBench has 325 problems. CoT vs non-CoT output tokens on miniF2F-test: 671B 6,751.9 vs 761.8; 7B 4,488.5 vs 442.6.
limits: CoT mode is more accurate than non-CoT but costs about 9x to 10x the output tokens. No explicit repair-by-error loop in this paper.
agent_relevance: Decomposition into subgoals is the 2025 form of a proof plan. The cost of reasoning mode is large.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: scaffolded data synthesis and self-correction
finding: The prover is trained to read the Lean compiler feedback on its own failed proof and write a corrected proof, up to 2 extra rounds within a 40K-token budget. RL mixes 50% whole-proof tasks with 50% first-round correction tasks.
numbers: MiniF2F: 32B reaches 88.1% pass@32, 90.4% with self-correction (about +2 points for both model sizes). 8B 84.6% at pass@32. PutnamBench: 43 solved at pass@32, 57 with self-correction; 86 at pass@184 with correction. DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B: 47 at pass@1024. In one analysis, pass@32 with correction averaged 92.7%, above 92.2% for no correction at pass@8192.
limits: The averaged-model result (92.7%) is a different setting from the headline 90.4%. Correction uses extra tokens, so the cost per sample rises.
agent_relevance: Measured evidence that compiler-fed revision raises pass rates at fixed sample counts, and that the lift is larger on harder problems (14 more on Putnam).

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover: deep and broad reasoning for automated theorem proving
finding: A whole-proof model that refines proofs using Lean compiler feedback, proved lemmas kept in a lemma pool, and self-summarisation of earlier attempts. Three settings: light (8-16 refinements), medium (outer plus inner refinement on hard lemmas), heavy (conjecture pool; days of search, thousands of lemmas).
numbers: 78.1% of formalised past IMO problems; MiniF2F-test 99.6% (previous best 92.2%); PutnamBench 331/657 (previous 86); CombiBench 30.0% (previous 10.0%); MiniCTX-v2 81.8% (o4-mini 44.3%). Light setting equals Pass@64-256 of budget. IMO 2022 P2 solved with refinement but needed Pass@8192 without it.
limits: The heavy setting uses days of compute, so the results are not equal-cost comparisons. Medium and heavy settings were run on problems left unsolved.
agent_relevance: Refinement beats sampling: one hard problem needed Pass@8192 without refinement. A lemma pool plus summary is a memory layer for REVISE.

source: Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard (2015) Analysis of patch plausibility and correctness for generate-and-validate program repair (as cited in Ringer et al. 2020)
finding: Cited in the QED at Large survey: many program repair tools output patches that pass the test suite but are wrong. The authors recommend using extra information such as specs or example patches.
numbers: Not read. Only the one-sentence summary in the survey was seen.
limits: Second-hand. Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Warns that a pass on weak checks is not a correct repair. Fits G3: validate on something the fix was not fitted to.

source: Melis & Siekmann (1999) Knowledge-based proof planning, Artificial Intelligence 115
finding: Proof planning in the OMEGA system with knowledge-based methods for mathematics, with control rules that choose among methods. Extends the Edinburgh idea beyond induction.
numbers: Not read. Listed from memory of the literature; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Verify title, year and claims before citing.
agent_relevance: Pointer for a later pass on multi-strategy proof planning.

source: Ireland & Bundy (1992) Using failure to guide inductive proof (Edinburgh DAI RP 613) - relation to other systems
finding: The paper claims rippling is a rational reconstruction of Boyer-Moore (nqthm) heuristics and that the critics let CLAM find proofs where nqthm cross-fertilisation and generalisation break down. Huet-Hullot completion proves the example but its use for lemma discovery is rare and less principled.
numbers: Claim only. No head-to-head count in the text read.
limits: Self-reported by the authors; no independent replication found in this session.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation: general search (completion) can also find the lemma but lacks the focus a plan gives.
